content: Dr. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the Director-General of the World Health Organization (WHO), has called for global action to eliminate cervical cancer. In August 2020, the Seventy-third World Health Assembly unanimously endorsed a global strategy to accelerate the elimination of cervical cancer as a public health problem. This strategy sets ambitious targets to be achieved by 2030, including vaccinating 90% of eligible girls against human papillomavirus (HPV), screening 70% of eligible women at least twice in their lifetimes, and ensuring effective treatment for 90% of women with positive screening results or cervical lesions, including palliative care when necessary. In alignment with this strategy, countries are revising their protocols for cervical cancer prevention, care, and treatment. Preventing cervical cancer is also critical to achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly those related to health (SDG 3) and gender equality (SDG 5). Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) refers to cellular changes in the transformation zone of the cervix, often caused by high-risk HPV infections, particularly strains 16 and 18, which are responsible for over 70% of cervical cancers. CIN 1 lesions, also known as low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions, are morphological indicators of HPV infections. Traditionally, cervical cancer screening has relied on cytology (the Papanicolaou test or Pap smear). Positive cytology results are confirmed through colposcopy, with treatment decisions guided by biopsy and histological diagnosis. Current and emerging screening approaches include HPV DNA testing, which detects high-risk HPV strains, and visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA). When ablative treatment is indicated, it is ideally performed during the same visit as the screening test (single-visit approach). However, in some settings, a second visit may be required (multiple-visit approach). If excisional treatment, such as large loop excision of the transformation zone (LLETZ), is unavailable on-site, women must be referred for further evaluation or treatment. Screening and treatment strategies are categorized into two main approaches: the screen-and-treat approach, where treatment is based solely on a positive primary screening test, and the screen, triage, and treat approach, where treatment decisions are based on both a positive primary screening test and a positive triage test, with or without histological confirmation. The WHO has updated its guidelines to reflect new evidence and developments in cervical cancer prevention. These updates aim to improve national strategies for screening and treatment, particularly for women living with HIV, who are at higher risk of cervical cancer. The guidelines emphasize evidence-based strategies, including HPV vaccination, screening, and treatment of pre-cancerous lesions, as well as palliative care for advanced cases. The guideline development process involved extensive collaboration among experts, including the Guideline Development Group (GDG), systematic review teams, and modeling teams. The recommendations were informed by systematic reviews, mathematical modeling, and stakeholder feedback. The updated guidelines also address the needs of diverse populations, including transgender men, non-binary individuals, and others with a female reproductive system, while using the term women for simplicity. The first phase focused on updating clinical algorithms for commonly used screening and triage strategies, while subsequent phases will evaluate additional evidence and develop implementation recommendations. The ultimate goal is to support countries in achieving the 2030 targets for cervical cancer elimination. The updated guidelines also highlight the importance of equity and accessibility in cervical cancer prevention services. They aim to provide clear, actionable recommendations for policymakers, healthcare providers, and individuals, ensuring that all people at risk for cervical cancer receive appropriate care, regardless of gender identity or other factors.
